ca_3_dream_wall.blurb: Dream Wall is one section of the Marble Caves limestone cliffs in far northern California, set on a ridgeline above the South Fork of the Trinity River. It is a tall face with only a handful of developed lines: eight in all, seven of them bolted sport routes and one top rope. Grades sit between 5.11 and 5.12, so this is a stop for climbers already comfortable leading in that range rather than a place to learn. The neighbouring walls hold many more routes if you want variety within the same ridge.

ca_canyon_hills.blurb: Canyon Hills is a small bouldering and top-rope spot among the housing tracts of Menifee in the Inland Empire. There are eight climbs in total: four boulder problems at V0 to V1, plus three top-rope lines from about 5.7 to 5.9 and a single trad line. Most boulders are short, and two of the top-rope lines have bolted anchors at roughly 25 feet. The stone varies, with some featureless, crumbly or sharp patches, though the top-rope lines are better. Bring your own pads and rope; this is a quick local session rather than a destination trip.

ca_school_bus_the.blurb: The School Bus is a single roadside granite boulder in Truckee, close to the Truckee River Legacy Trail and the I-80 corridor near Lake Tahoe. It carries eight problems, all easy to moderate: one at the V-easy end, a couple at V0, and most of the rest between V1 and V2. The boulder stands only a short distance from the pavement, so a session here takes little planning and suits warm-ups, beginners or a quick stop on a drive through town. A crash pad and a spotter are all you need.

ca_dark_side_2.blurb: Dark Side is a dome-shaped section of the Dark Crown cliffs, high above Rodeo Flat on the Kern Plateau in the southern Sierra. It has eight short routes, split evenly between sport and trad. Most fall in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, with a single 5.7 and one hard 5.12 at the top end. Dark Crown as a whole mixes slabs with overhanging cracks and has bolted and gear lines in about equal numbers, so carry a trad rack as well as quickdraws.

ca_sugar_mountain.blurb: Sugar Mountain is a small crag in Rock Creek, in the eastern Sierra between Bishop and Mammoth Lakes, sitting up a drainage between the Iris Slab and Gong Show sectors. It has eight trad routes, mostly 5.9 to 5.10 with one 5.7 and a single 5.11 near the top. The granite faces are short, and the crag sees far fewer visitors than its neighbours; bring a full rack. The walk in is longer than at the nearby cliffs, and the stream makes the route past Iris Slab the practical choice.

ca_alpentine_wall.blurb: Alpentine Wall is a section of Campfire Crag in the Indian Cove area of Joshua Tree National Park. It juts out a little from the main south face and feels like a crag of its own. It holds eight trad routes from about 5.6 up to a single 5.12 face climb, with the bulk in the 5.7 to 5.10 range. Most lines are moderate cracks where the placements take some thought, which makes it a decent pick for climbers building trad skills. Campfire Crag overall draws less traffic than the nearby Pixie Rock and Short Wall.

ca_2_main_right.blurb: Main - Right is the shorter, right-hand part of School Rock, a big low-angle slab on Donner Summit near Lake Tahoe. It holds eight routes: four trad, three sport and one top rope. Grades run from about 5.7 up to 5.11, with most in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, so it is more demanding than the easier sections of the same formation. A trail runs along the base of the wall, which keeps the walk from the car short, and the sport and top-rope lines make it workable without a full rack.

ca_condor_rock.blurb: Condor Rock is a compact crag in the Indian Cove section of Joshua Tree National Park, facing King Otto's Castle across the road. It has eight routes, almost all trad, plus one top-rope line. Six of them sit at 5.10, with one 5.8 and one 5.12 stemming corner at the harder end. A straight-in crack is one of the better-known lines. The walk in is short, and the crag sits away from the busier campground formations. Bring a standard trad rack and a few extra cams for the cracks.
